```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(dinarch)
```

`dinarch` fits Dynamic Innovation Negative Binomial ARCH (NB-DINARCH) models
to count time series: an autoregressive negative-binomial model where the
mean depends on past counts and, optionally, covariates.

## Simulate some data

`dinarch_simulate()` generates a count series with a given autoregressive
coefficient `b`, dispersion `phi`, and (optionally) covariate effects
specified via a model formula.

```{r}
set.seed(2)
n <- 200
gdp <- rnorm(n)

dat <- dinarch_simulate(
  n = n, b = 0.3, phi = 8,
  formula = ~gdp, covariates = data.frame(gdp = gdp),
  beta = c(log(4), 0.5),
  seed = 2
)

dat$gdp <- gdp
head(dat)
```

## Fit the model

`dinarch_fit_ml()` fits the model by maximum likelihood. `formula` specifies
how covariates enter the mean (here, a single `gdp` effect plus an
intercept); `n_lags` sets the number of autoregressive lags.

```{r}
fit <- dinarch_fit_ml(dat, y = "y", time = "time", formula = ~gdp, n_lags = 1)
fit
summary(fit)
```

`summary()` reports standard errors and confidence intervals alongside the
point estimates.

## Predict forward

`predict()` draws samples from the fitted model's predictive distribution -
`horizon` sets how many periods ahead, `nsim` how many draws. A fit object
stores no data of its own, so `predict()` always takes the historical data
to project from explicitly - this keeps it clear which data a projection is
built from, and lets you project the same fit forward from updated data
without refitting. Covariates default to their last observed value in `data`.

```{r}
pred <- predict(fit, dat, horizon = 50, nsim = 500, seed = 2)
pred
```

The result has one row per `(id, time, sim)` observation: `dat`'s historical
rows (repeated once per replicate) plus the simulated/forecast draws, marked
by the `pred` column (`TRUE` for simulated/forecast draws) - so
`pred[sim == 1]` is always one complete, continuously-indexed series
(history through the forecast).

`summary()` collapses the draws into the mean and quantiles of `y` over
blocks of consecutive periods: one row for the observed history
(`pred == FALSE`), and the simulated window (`pred == TRUE`) split into
`nsplit` blocks, each labelled by its inclusive `start`/`end` time
(`nsplit = NULL` gives one row per period). `plot()` shows the draws as a
shaded band (pass `type = "spaghetti"` to instead draw every draw as its
own thin line).

```{r}
summary(pred)
```


```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
plot(pred[sim == sample.int(500, 1)], type = "spaghetti") # Plot a random simulation
```

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
plot(pred, probs = c(0.025, 0.975)) # Plot 95% prediction interval
```

Calling `predict()` with `horizon = NULL` (the default) instead replays the
fitted model in-sample, useful as a quick check that the fitted dynamics
look reasonable against the data the model was fit to.

```{r}
pred_insample <- predict(fit, dat, horizon = NULL, nsim = 500, seed = 2)
plot(pred_insample, probs = c(0.025, 0.975)) # Plot 95% prediction interval
```


`predict()` is a thin convenience wrapper around the more general
`dinarch_project()`, which additionally supports scenario-style
overrides (`new_data` for alternative covariate paths, `new_para` for
per-period parameter overrides) - see below.

## Scenario: transitioning between two fits

Suppose a second fit represents a different regime - `dinarch_transition()`
builds a `new_para` table that moves the model from one fit to another
over the forecast horizon, for scenarios like "assume the dynamics
gradually shift from `fit`'s regime to `fit_b`'s". Rather than
interpolating each raw coefficient separately, it interpolates
interpretable quantities - persistence `sum(b)`, the lag shares, the
covariate slopes, `1/phi`, and the log long-run mean at each id's last
observed covariate values - and solves the intercept to match, so e.g.
the long-run mean doesn't dip mid-path between two equal-mean regimes:

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
sim_b <- dinarch_simulate(
  n = n, b = 0.15, phi = 0.2,
  formula = ~gdp, covariates = data.frame(gdp = gdp),
  beta = c(log(15), 0.2), seed = 3
)
dat_b <- data.frame(y = sim_b$y, time = sim_b$time, gdp = gdp)
fit_b <- dinarch_fit_ml(dat_b, y = "y", time = "time", formula = ~gdp, n_lags = 1)
h <- 50

new_para <- dinarch_transition(fit_from = fit, fit_to = fit_b, data = dat, horizon = h, shape = "sigmoid")
scenario <- dinarch_project(fit, dat, horizon = h, nsim = 500, new_para = new_para, seed = 2)
plot(scenario)
```

With `shape = "linear"`, the last forecast period matches `fit_b`'s
parameters exactly; the default sigmoid gets to within weight
`plogis(9)` (about 0.99988) of them. `fit` and `fit_b` must share
`n_lags` and the same `beta` coefficient names (i.e. the same `formula`,
which must include an intercept). For Bayesian fits, `nsim` (with the
same value passed to `dinarch_project()`) builds one transition per
replicate from independent posterior draws, propagating parameter
uncertainty into the scenario.

## Multiple series: unpooled fits, combined for plotting

`dinarch_fit_ml()`/`dinarch_fit_bayes()` accept an `id` column to *pool*
several series into one shared set of coefficients (lags never cross an
id boundary, but `b`/`phi`/`beta` are shared across every id). Sometimes
you instead want each series fit *separately*, with its own dynamics -
that's just calling the fit function once per series and combining the
resulting `dinarch_project()` calls afterward.

```{r}
ids <- c("A", "B", "C")
params <- list(
  A = list(n = 60, b = 0.15, phi = 0.2,  beta = log(15)),
  B = list(n = 60, b = 0.2, phi = 2,  beta = log(10)),
  C = list(n = 60, b = 0.3, phi = 8, beta = log(4))
)

dat_list <- Map(function(g, p) {
  s <- dinarch_simulate(
    n = p$n, 
    b = p$b, 
    phi = p$phi, 
    beta = p$beta,
    seed = which(ids == g))
  data.frame(y = s$y, time = s$time, id = g)
}, ids, params)

fits <- Map(function(g) dinarch_fit_ml(dat_list[[g]], n_lags = 1, vcov = FALSE), ids)
```

Project each series from its own fit and its own data, then combine them
with `as_dinarch_project()`: given a list of projections it row-binds them
and reattaches the `"dinarch_project"` class (which a plain `rbind()`/
`data.table::rbindlist()` drops), after checking the result still has the
shape `plot()`/`summary()` expect - including that no two series share an
`id`.

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
proj_list <- Map(function(g) {
  dinarch_project(fits[[g]], dat_list[[g]], id = "id", horizon = 50, nsim = 100, seed = 4)
}, ids)

combined <- as_dinarch_project(proj_list)

plot(combined, type = "spaghetti")  # facets by id automatically, since there's more than one
summary(combined)
```

The same trick composes with `dinarch_transition()`: interpolate
every other series' dynamics toward one reference series' regime, then
combine the resulting per-series projections the same way.

```{r, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4}
end_id <- "A"
fit_end <- fits[[end_id]]

proj_interp_list <- lapply(setdiff(ids, end_id), function(g) {
  new_para <- dinarch_transition(fits[[g]], fit_end, dat_list[[g]], horizon = 50)
  dinarch_project(fits[[g]], dat_list[[g]], id = "id", horizon = 50, nsim = 100,
                   new_para = new_para, seed = 5)
})

combined_interp <- as_dinarch_project(proj_interp_list)

plot(combined_interp)
```

## Bayesian estimation

`dinarch_fit_bayes()` fits the same model via Stan/HMC instead of maximum
likelihood (requires the `rstan` package), and works as a drop-in
replacement for `dinarch_fit_ml()` in the calls above.
